summary: First English narrative for the 1976 swine flu immunization decision, written from the case's primary-source facts (Neustadt-Fineberg chronology; Ford Library 22 March 1976 meeting file).

narrative.hook: A new flu virus, related to the one blamed for the 1918 pandemic, has killed an Army recruit in New Jersey and has not been found spreading anywhere else. You have about two weeks to tell the vaccine makers whether to start producing enough for every American.
narrative.short_setup: On 4 February 1976, Private David Lewis left his sick bed at Fort Dix, New Jersey, joined a five-mile night march, collapsed and died. Throat washings from Fort Dix recruits had already been sent for testing, and by mid-February the Center for Disease Control had confirmed that some contained a swine-type influenza virus, A/New Jersey/76. The Army's blood surveys suggested as many as 500 recruits may have been exposed. A nationwide search turned up a handful of other swine-flu infections in five states, but in every case except one doubtful one in Virginia, the person had been in contact with pigs. No outbreak was found outside Fort Dix. On 13 March, CDC director David Sencer finished a memorandum, signed by Assistant Secretary for Health Theodore Cooper, recommending a federal program to immunize the entire population. On 22 March it reached President Gerald Ford in the Cabinet Room, alongside a budget office briefing that listed what nobody knew.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The case for vaccinating everyone rested on timing and on the shape of the risk. HEW's memorandum argued that this was a 'go or no go' situation: to protect some 213 million people, a program would have to be running at full scale by the beginning of September and finished by the end of November, and manufacturers needed a go-ahead within about two weeks. Vaccine could not be conjured once a pandemic was under way. The memo noted that the virus was antigenically related to the one implicated in the 1918-1919 pandemic, that Americans under 50 were probably susceptible, and that severe flu epidemics had come at roughly ten-year intervals, the last in 1968-69. Against that, the cost was bounded and known: about $134 million. The memo put the logic in one line: the administration 'can tolerate unnecessary health expenditures better than unnecessary death and illness.' The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices had agreed on 10 March that major action was needed.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for making the vaccine but holding back the mass campaign rested on how thin the evidence was. Person-to-person spread had been proven at exactly one place, an Army post. The budget office's briefing for the 22 March meeting recorded that HEW's own epidemiologists had called the probability of an epidemic 'unknown.' The vaccine would do nothing against the ordinary flu strains of recent years, and a mutated swine virus might slip past it. A pandemic today might not resemble 1918, before antibiotics. And the briefing asked a question about precedent: if the government vaccinated everyone this year and nothing happened, would it have to do the same every year? Stockpiling was not a fringe idea. CDC staff had discussed it at some length on 9 March, and it had come up at the advisory committee the next day. Holding vaccine in reserve, protecting the elderly and chronically ill as usual, and watching for a second outbreak would keep the insurance without exposing tens of millions of people to a new vaccine's unknown risks.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Ford did not decide on 22 March. He said he wanted to hear from leading scientists first, and on 24 March he met a panel that included both Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin. Afterwards he went before television cameras, recommended that every American be vaccinated, and asked Congress for $135 million, which he signed into law on 15 April. The reasoning was the reasoning of the HEW memorandum: the possibility of a 1918-type pandemic could not be ruled out, the lead time for vaccine left no room to wait for proof, and the cost of acting unnecessarily was smaller than the cost of failing to act. The memorandum had framed the choice as go or no go and did not present stockpiling to the President as a separate alternative; its four options were no action, a minimum federal response, a fully government-run program, and the combined public-private program it recommended.
narrative.outcome_story: The program stalled almost at once over liability. Insurers refused to cover the vaccine makers, and the makers would not proceed without federal protection, until Congress passed and Ford signed a special tort-claims law on 12 August. In early August, a mysterious outbreak in Philadelphia briefly raised fears that swine flu had arrived; within days influenza was ruled out. The first shots were given on 1 October. On 11 October three elderly people died shortly after being vaccinated at the same Pittsburgh clinic, and health officials in nine states suspended vaccination until investigators found no link to the vaccine; on 14 October Ford and his family were vaccinated in front of television cameras. Participation lagged badly. Then reports of Guillain-Barre syndrome, a rare paralytic illness, began to accumulate among the vaccinated. By 14 December CDC counted 54 cases in 10 states, 30 of them in people who had received the shot. On 16 December, after a conference call with outside experts, the program was suspended with the President's approval. More than 40 million people had been vaccinated. The pandemic never came.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
It is tempting to read this as a simple error: the government vaccinated tens of millions of people against a pandemic that never happened, and some of them were harmed. But the outcome tells you less about the decision than it seems to. Start with what was knowable in March 1976. The probability of a pandemic was genuinely unknown, and the documents say so. The stakes were genuinely lopsided: a bounded, known cost against a possibility that, if it came, would be measured in lives at a national scale. And the lead time was a hard constraint, not a rhetorical one. Vaccine for 200 million people could not be produced and delivered after an epidemic had already begun. On those terms, deciding to act was defensible, and Ford's step of hearing from independent scientists before announcing was a sound one.

The weaknesses are in how the uncertainty was handled, not in the decision to act. The President received two incompatible descriptions of the same risk on the same day: HEW's memo said there was a 'strong possibility' of widespread swine flu, while the budget office's briefing said HEW's epidemiologists called the probability 'unknown.' Stockpiling, which CDC staff and the advisory committee had discussed, was not put in front of him as a separate choice; the memo framed the question as go or no go. And the recommendation committed to immunizing the whole population with no stated point at which the decision would be revisited if the virus failed to reappear. A decision built to change course as evidence arrived, for example producing at full speed while setting a date to decide on mass vaccination, might have kept most of the protection with less exposure.

The outcome mixes luck with things that were foreseeable. That the virus never spread was luck in the plain sense: nobody could have known it in March. The Guillain-Barre signal was not something anyone had predicted. But the liability collapse that delayed the program by months was flagged before Fort Dix: in January 1976, a CDC official had warned HEW's Secretary that liability problems might drive vaccine makers out of the business. That risk was on paper and still caught the program unprepared. The fair verdict is a reasonable bet, made under real time pressure, that went badly, partly through bad luck and partly through risks that were visible and not managed.
narrative.decision_principle: When the evidence you need will arrive only after you must commit, committing can be right; but say in advance what new evidence would make you stop, and do not let the case for acting turn an unknown probability into a confident one.
narrative.longform_story:
On the night of 4 February 1976, at Fort Dix in New Jersey, a recruit named David Lewis got out of the bed he had been confined to and went on a five-mile march with his platoon. He collapsed on the way and died. It was, at that moment, a sad but not a historic event. Respiratory illness had been running through the camp for weeks, and the Army had assumed it was the usual adenovirus.

It was not. Throat washings from sick recruits had gone to the New Jersey state laboratory, and some of the samples could not be typed. They went on to the Center for Disease Control in Atlanta, and on 12 and 13 February CDC's scientists confirmed what they were looking at: a swine-type influenza virus, which they designated A/New Jersey/76. A sample taken from Lewis was among them. On 14 February an emergency meeting at CDC brought together the Army, the state, the federal vaccine regulators and the National Institutes of Health. On 19 February CDC announced the finding to the press.

What made the finding alarming was its family resemblance. HEW's own later memorandum described the virus as antigenically related to the one implicated in the 1918-1919 pandemic, which, in the memo's figure, had killed 450,000 Americans. People under 50 had never been exposed to anything like it and were probably susceptible. Severe flu epidemics had come at roughly ten-year intervals; the last had been in 1968-69. If the Fort Dix virus was the start of something, the timing fitted.

But was it the start of something? Over the following weeks, CDC searched the country. It found a few other swine-flu infections, in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Mississippi, and in every case but one doubtful Virginia case the person had worked with or been near pigs. Swine flu passing from pigs to farmers was known; it had happened before without spreading further. Inside Fort Dix the virus had clearly passed from person to person, and Army blood surveys suggested as many as 500 recruits might have been exposed. Outside the gates, nothing.

That was the evidence when the decision had to be made, and the calendar would not wait for more. Flu vaccine is grown in eggs, and making enough for an entire country takes months. CDC's director, David Sencer, laid out the timetable in a memorandum he finished on 13 March and sent up under the signature of the Assistant Secretary for Health, Theodore Cooper. To vaccinate some 213 million people, the program would have to be in full operation by the beginning of September and done by the end of November. 'The situation is one of "go or no go,"' it said. 'A decision must be made now.'

The memo set out four alternatives: do nothing beyond the routine; a minimum federal response that left most of the work to industry and the market; a fully government-run campaign; or a combined public-private program costing about $134 million, which it recommended. It was candid about the case for doing nothing; among the arguments listed in favor was that the pandemic might not occur and the money would be saved. But its conclusion rested on an asymmetry: the administration 'can tolerate unnecessary health expenditures better than unnecessary death and illness, particularly if a flu pandemic should occur.'

Not everyone in the building saw the evidence the same way. On 22 March the memo reached President Gerald Ford at a thirty-minute meeting in the Cabinet Room, together with a briefing from his budget director, James Lynn. The briefing's first attachment was a list titled 'Uncertainties Surrounding a Federal Mass Swine Influenza Immunization Program.' It noted that person-to-person transmission had been proven in only one location. It said HEW's epidemiologists had stated that the probability of an epidemic was 'unknown.' It pointed out that the vaccine would do nothing against the ordinary flu strains of recent years, and that a mutated swine virus might evade it. It suggested that a modern pandemic might not resemble the one before antibiotics. And it asked a question about precedent: if the government mounted a massive effort this year and nothing happened, would it have to do so every year?

There was also a middle path that never reached the President as a formal option. On 9 March, before the advisory committee met, Sencer and his staff had discussed stockpiling vaccine at some length. At the committee's meeting the next day, stockpiling was mentioned briefly; the members agreed that major action was needed. The idea was simple: manufacture the vaccine, keep it in reserve, protect the elderly and chronically ill as usual, and start the mass campaign only if swine flu began to spread. Its weakness was the same calendar that drove the memo. If you waited for proof, you might start too late.

Ford did not decide that morning. He asked to hear from the country's leading scientists, and on 24 March he met a panel that included Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin. After the meeting he went before the television cameras, recommended that every American be vaccinated, and asked Congress for $135 million. Congress moved quickly, and Ford signed the money into law on 15 April.

Then the program ran into a problem that had been visible before Fort Dix. In January 1976 a CDC official had warned that liability fears might drive vaccine makers out of the business. Now insurers told the manufacturers they would not cover claims arising from the swine flu program, and the manufacturers would not proceed without protection. The standoff lasted through the spring and summer, until Congress passed a law making the federal government answerable for claims, which Ford signed on 12 August. In early August a mysterious outbreak among people who had attended a convention in Philadelphia briefly raised fears that swine flu had arrived; within days investigators had ruled out influenza.

The first shots were given on 1 October. Ten days later, three elderly people died shortly after being vaccinated at the same clinic in Pittsburgh. Health officials in nine states suspended vaccination while the deaths were investigated, and resumed when no link to the vaccine was found. On 14 October Ford and his family rolled up their sleeves in front of the cameras. Public enthusiasm, though, was draining away. By mid-November only four project areas had vaccinated more than half their target population, and a New York Times poll found that more than half of unvaccinated New Yorkers thought the shot was unnecessary.

In November a case of Guillain-Barre syndrome, a rare illness that can cause paralysis, was reported in a vaccinated person in Minnesota. More followed. By 14 December CDC had counted 54 cases in 10 states, 30 of them in people who had received the swine flu shot. Sencer held three conference calls with outside experts in four days. On 16 December they recommended a pause to investigate, Cooper consulted the Secretary and the White House, and the President approved. More than 40 million Americans had been vaccinated. The next day CDC's William Foege told a Senate subcommittee that the incidence of Guillain-Barre among the vaccinated appeared to be about four times normal; in January 1977 the advisory committee put the added risk at roughly one case per 100,000 to 200,000 vaccinations.

The swine flu pandemic never came. The virus never spread from person to person beyond Fort Dix; the few further infections found that winter showed no human-to-human spread, and several were traced to pigs. On 30 December Ford said he agreed with the suspension but defended the decision he had made in March. A new administration took office in January. By early February 1977 the Justice Department reported 104 damage claims, worth almost $11 million, filed against the federal government under the August law. That month the new Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, Joseph Califano, replaced Sencer as head of CDC. Sencer would later write, with the head of the 1976 program, that the government had 'wisely opted to put protection of the public first.' HEW commissioned Richard Neustadt and Harvey Fineberg to review the episode; their report, The Swine Flu Affair, was published in 1978.

The tempting lesson is that the government overreacted. The harder one is that the decision and the outcome have to be judged separately. In March 1976 nobody knew whether the virus would spread, and the vaccine could not wait to find out. What can fairly be questioned is how the uncertainty was carried: two incompatible descriptions of the same risk on the President's desk on the same day, a middle path that was discussed but not put to him, and a plan to vaccinate everyone with no stated moment to stop and look again. The liability crisis that cost the program months had been foreseen in January. The virus that never spread, and the side effect nobody predicted, were not things anyone could have known.
